title: What I learned building my first game with AI tools: A 38-year-old accountant's journey to shipping a multiplayer mobile game
author: Jonathan_Bjerk
selftext:
I'm not a developer. I'm a 38-year-old accountant from Norway who had never written code before 2024. Six months and 500+ hours later, I shipped Curve Clash - a real-time multiplayer mobile game that hit #4 in Family Games in my country.

I'm sharing this because I think there are useful lessons here, even for experienced devs.

**The tools I used:**

* **Claude & ChatGPT**: For code generation, debugging, and architecture decisions
* **Cursor**: As my IDE with AI integration
* **Flutter + Firebase**: The actual tech stack

**What worked:**

1. **"Vibe coding" is real** \- I could describe what I wanted ("make the curves leave a trail that other players can collide with") and iterate until it worked. The AI understood game logic surprisingly well.
2. **Understanding > Writing** \- I can't write a Flutter function from scratch. But I learned to read code, understand why it breaks, and describe fixes. That's enough to ship.
3. **Architecture matters more than syntax** \- The hardest bugs weren't code problems, they were architecture problems. AI helped me refactor toward better patterns once I understood what was wrong.
4. **Real-time multiplayer is hard** \- Firebase works, but latency compensation, state sync, and edge cases took 40% of my time. If I did it again, I might use a dedicated multiplayer backend.

**What I'd do differently:**

1. **Test on more devices earlier** \- Performance issues on older Android phones caught me late
2. **Build analytics first** \- I added proper event tracking too late
3. **Scope smaller** \- I built 4 game modes when 1 polished mode would have been better for launch

**The game:** Curve Clash is a multiplayer snake game inspired by "Achtung die Kurve" (90s LAN party classic). Free with a $3 Pro upgrade.

Not here to promote - genuinely curious if other devs have tried AI-assisted development and what your experience was like.

*Disclosure: This is my own game. Happy to answer questions about the technical side or the AI workflow.*

replies.author: Jonathan_Bjerk
replies.body:
Honestly? I didn't know Unity existed when I started 😅

I asked AI "how do I build a mobile game" and it suggested Flutter since it's good for cross-platform. By the time I learned Unity might be better for games, I was already deep into Flutter.

Turns out Flutter was actually decent for this – Unity's web support on mobile browsers was pretty limited until recently. For a simple 2D game, Flutter worked fine. But yeah, for anything bigger I'd probably look into Unity or Godot.

comments.author: Revelation12Studios
comments.body:
Nice! Did life get in the way for it to take you six months to make this or was there just a ton of work involved to finish it?

I worked on a card game RPG for a few months using Gemini but put it on hold and for the past couple months been using Gemini to make a mech shooter-looter RPG to eventually upload to Reddit.

replies.author: Jonathan_Bjerk
replies.body:
Both! Full-time job + family, so evenings and weekends only. But also a ton of work – about 500 hours total.

Flutter is Google's framework for building cross-platform apps. You write one codebase (in Dart) and it compiles to iOS, Android, and web. It has "hot reload" so you see changes instantly while coding – super helpful for iterating fast.

Mech shooter-looter RPG sounds awesome – way more ambitious than my snake game! Good luck with it, and feel free to DM if you want to compare notes on the AI workflow 🤖

comments.author: IndubitablyNerdy
comments.body:
1. **Understanding > Writing** \- I can't write a Flutter function from scratch. But I learned to read code, understand why it breaks, and describe fixes. That's enough to ship.

I think that this is the key, you need to have some understanding at least at a basic level to help with troubelshooting, finding bugs and make an architecture that is not too clunky\\unoptimized. This give you an edge compared to just using the AI output blindly and I imagine that the more experienced you are the more you can leverage the support you get from AI. Also the models have really improved in 2025 compared to 2024, 

I have been working on and off on a game for fun (likely one tha twill never reach a finished state as it is just for personal entertainment pretty much, but who knows right?) I rely on AI from time to time when I am struck and would otherwise have checked stack overflow or searched for online in general and in the last 6ish months I have noticed marked improvements in how usable the Ai suggestions are.

replies.author: Jonathan_Bjerk
replies.body:
Exactly – understanding gives you an edge. Blindly copy-pasting AI output gets you stuck fast.

And yeah, the models in 2026 are way better than when I started in mid-2025. The difference is noticeable.

Good luck with your game! Even if it stays a personal project, the learning is worth it 🎮

comments.author: Kallekalif
comments.body: as someone with similar aspirations, same age group, situation and even country, this is very inspiring! Can you say anything about how you got visibility and scaled the game? i mean i have the impression that mobile games are difficult to market and get out there, and perhaps even more difficult to make revenue on? Also any other thought or tips for someone looking to making succesful games in a similar situation?

replies.author: Jonathan_Bjerk
replies.body:
Honestly, I'm still figuring it out! 1,150 players sounds okay but organic growth is slow. Most active players are still people I know personally.

What I've done:
- Daily posts on TikTok/Instagram for 140+ days (mixed results)
- This Reddit post is my first real attempt here
- Web version at curveclash.com so people can try instantly without downloading

What I've learned:
- Authentic behind-the-scenes content beats polished ads
- TikTok gets more views but conversion to downloads is tough
- Mobile game marketing is HARD – you're right about that

Revenue is tiny so far – a few dollars from ads and Pro upgrades. Not quitting my day job anytime soon 😅

Tip: Get beta testers early. I had friends and family testing for months before launch – saved me from a lot of embarrassing bugs.

Lykke til! 🇳🇴

comments.author: jarofgoodness
comments.body:
Working on several; games right now using Grok. Two of them also use phaser. These are javascript browser games meant to eventually be played on android devices after wrapping. 

Anyway, I also have a limited understanding of code. I can write html webpages and visual basic and I know a little javascript. My biggest complaint in working this way- and I hate to bitch about this since I am getting good results and it's free after all- is Grok often misses the boat completely on debugging. Half the time the issue ends up being some bit of code Grok changed while we were working on something else because it was trying to streamline the code and be helpful. It ends up screwing something up and then can't figure out why it isn't working, offers a handful of fixes none of which fix the problem and half of which cause some other problem. 

At the same time it demonstrates a great ability to do a large amount of very good coding in a short amount of time, so I can't really complain. I couldn't have done this without AI but damn every project has moments where I'm thinking "I could have done this myself in 10 minutes with visual basic, instead it's taken two days." 

By the way, if anyone knows a great resource for AI generated or royalty free sound effects for games let me know. I looked over the usual suspects today and am unsatisfied.
